text.p: The Swedish crown swam against the tide of a weakening mark during Europe's morning, pressured by corporate flows and stock moves, traders and analysts said.

"It's related to the equity market -- partly it's dividend payouts this week and next week, and there are coupon payments next week...these are heavy weeks of outflows," said Peter Lindquist, Nordic economist at HSBC Markets in Stockholm.
The sell-off in the Swedish stock market over the last few days had also depressed the crown, Lindquist added.
The Swedish crown slid to 4.5330/60 per mark by 1037 GMT from late Monday's European level of 4.5075/05.
The crown earlier touched 4.5375, its weakest level against the mark since April 4.

"Some big Swedish companies have got some share dividends -- and there are some bond coupons that have been paid -- and they're not reinvesting in Sweden, so they're selling Sweden and buying other foreign currencies," said Peter Heath, senior dealer at Merita Bank in London.
The market was thin, however, ahead of May Day and month-end, Heath said.
Elsewhere, the mark was generally softer on the crosses as a robust dollar/mark spilled over into Europe.
The German currency fell to 991.45/85 Italian lire and 3.3705/09 French francs from its previous closing rates here of 992.70/2.10 and 3.3716/19 respectively.
The market kept its eyes on France, where the ruling centre-right coalition set out its stall for the May 25/June 1 parliamentary election.

In its manifesto, the RPR-UDF alliance pledged to stabilise public spending, pursue tax cuts and promote negotiations on shorter working hours. It promised to modernise the state, free up private initiative, renovate the social system and make France "the motor of a citizens' Europe".

With the French franc highly vulnerable to market fears that the Socialists could seize power in the election -- and potentially launch less EMU-friendly policies -- players were awaiting today's meeting between Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and his Communist counterpart Robert Hue at 1345 GMT.
Jospin has said he would be willing to rule with the Communists, but they should accept Socialist policies.

The Socialists favour a single currency, although they have set conditions and refused further austerity measures if these were needed to reach the strict budget deficit criterion for European monetary union.
The Communists oppose the euro and want a referendum on the issue.
